item.title: Three minute battery cell health check could transform recycling and second-life potential
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Researchers at UNSW, Sydney have developed a battery health test that is 95.5% faster than existing testing, over 80% cheaper, and has the potential to both increase second-life battery use and keep significant battery waste from landfill.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers from the University of New South Wales (UNSW), Sydney have developed a prototype to test battery health, that is 95.5% faster than existing testing and over 80% cheaper, with implications for reducing landfill and improving second-life use.

Designed to work with the management systems already used by recyclers and energy storage operators, the platform will assess the three main lithium-ion chemistries used in electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage: lithium iron phosphate (LFP), nickel cobalt aluminium (NCA) and nickel manganese cobalt (NMC).

Current used-battery testing relies on an approximately 10-hour full charge-discharge process, which can lead to overheating and fire if damaged batteries endure hours of high-stress cycling. It also costs around $120 (USD 85) per EV battery pack.

Instead, the UNSW prototype platform uses short electrical pulses through each battery cell, and measures how cells respond. Statistical models then estimate the battery’s health in under three minutes per cell, with lab testing showing more than 90% accuracy. The target cost is under $25.

UNSW School of Systems and Computing Associate Professor Huadong Mo said as more electric vehicles (EVs) reach the end of their life, Australia has a real opportunity to build a local second-life battery industry, with retired batteries supporting grid and comunity energy storage.

“Up to 95% of a battery’s components can be recovered, some even to make new batteries. Yet only a small fraction of lithium-ion batteries in Australia are collected for recycling today,” Mo said.

The researchers have partnered with Malaysia-headquartered battery recycling and lifecycle management company DY New Energy on a $1.3 million project to test the new technology on more than 500 batteries in real-world conditions.

Before piloting it in recycling facilities and second-life battery storage systems, the DY and UNSW researchers will develop and test a machine learning-powered decision engine that recommends whether retired batteries should be reused or recycled.

A Battery Management System (iBMS) module will then integrate insights directly into battery systems for real-time monitoring and decision support.

UNSW School of Mathematics and Statistics, and Research Lead Dr Ziyang Lyu said recyclers rarely receive neatly sorted batches.

“One day it might be LFP cells, the next a mix of nickel-based chemistries from different manufacturers. We’ve designed our models to handle that variety, so the platform works with the batteries operators actually receive, not just ideal lab samples,” Lyu said.

Dr Lyu said the technology may also play a role in managing the growing number of batteries used in stationary energy storage systems.

“This technology could also support the future reuse and recycling of Australia’s rapidly expanding fleet of stationary energy storage systems, contributing to a more sustainable and circular battery economy.”

The project is also supported through the Trailblazer for Recycling and Clean Energy (TRaCE) Lab to Market Fund.

DY New Energy announced 13 November 2026 it will partner with the Australian Research Council’s (ARC’s) Fire Resilience Infrastructure, Assets and Safety Advancements (FRIASA) Hub to advance safe and scalable battery recycling.

item.title: Predicting power output from artistic BIPV pixel by pixel
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: Researchers have developed a model linking artwork colors to power output and potential hot-spot risks in colored BIPV arrays. Simulations of 50 masterpieces show how selectively darkening bright pixels can improve electrical performance.
item.content:encoded:
ASouth Korean research team has developed a novel model to predict power output and hot-spot risk in colored building-integrated PV (c-BIPV) systems featuring artistic images.

The researchers modeled PV arrays displaying 50 masterpieces, including Johannes Vermeer’s Girl with a Pearl Earring and Vincent van Gogh’s Café Terrace at Night.

“Unlike a uniformly colored module, an image-based array contains many differently colored cells. Because each color requires a different optical reflection profile, the photocurrent generated by each cell can vary across the array,” corresponding author Hyung-Jun Song told pv magazine.

“This spatial mismatch can reduce power output and, under certain bypass-diode configurations, expose cells to reverse bias and hot-spot risk.”

The novelty of the research, Song added, lies in directly linking the visual characteristics of a candidate image to the electrical performance and reliability of the entire PV array.

“For every pixel, we estimated the minimum-loss selective-reflection spectrum needed to reproduce its color and calculated the resulting photocurrent. We then used equivalent-circuit simulations to evaluate the series-connected array under different bypass-diode configurations,” he explained.

In its work, the group has converted each of the 50 artworks into a 36 × 36-pixel mosaic, with each of the 1,296 pixels representing an individual series-connected PV cell.

They assigned each pixel the average color of its corresponding image region. For each color, they calculated an ideal dual-band selective-reflection spectrum, selecting the reflection-band parameters that most closely reproduced the target color.

They then calculated the photocurrent generated from the sunlight transmitted through the colored layer, accounting for the underlying cell’s wavelength-dependent internal quantum efficiency.

Using a single-diode equivalent circuit calibrated to commercial TOPCon cells, they modeled each cell’s current-voltage characteristics at 300 K. They simulated the fully series-connected array in LTspice.

The simulations compared configurations without bypass diodes and with one diode protecting between one and 36 cells, assessing maximum power output and the number of cells operating under reverse bias at the maximum power point as an indicator of potential hot-spot risk.

“One of the most surprising findings was that the overall brightness or colorfulness of an image does not necessarily determine its photovoltaic performance. Instead, the spatial distribution of brightness plays a much more important role,” Song said about the results.

For example, the simulated array displaying Café Terrace at Night achieved 91.7% of the power output of an equivalent black reference array without bypass diodes, compared with 74.3% for Girl with a Pearl Earring.

“We found that even a small number of extremely bright pixels can limit the power output of an entire series-connected PV array,” the researcher added.

“We also identified an interesting trade-off associated with bypass diodes: installing more diodes can improve power output, but it may simultaneously increase reverse-bias conditions and the associated hot-spot risk.”

For Girl with a Pearl Earring, installing one bypass diode per cell increased normalised power from 74.3% to 84.4% of the black reference array’s output, a 13.6% relative improvement.

However, 24 of the 1,296 cells entered reverse bias at the maximum power point. Selectively darkening those 24 pixels instead raised normalised power to 84.8% without bypass diodes, while avoiding reverse-biased cells under the simulated conditions.

“Based on these findings, we developed a screening framework that classifies artistic images according to their expected power performance and hot-spot risk, using only two image-derived parameters: the brightest pixel and the overall brightness variation,” the academic added.

“The framework was further examined using additional images, demonstrating its potential to assess the electrical suitability of candidate artwork without requiring a full circuit-level simulation for every image.”

Concluding, Song said that his team is planning a few follow-up studies. These include incorporating measured reflectance spectra into a more realistic optical model, expanding the image database, and developing an AI-assisted tool to assess uploaded images and suggest modifications that improve power output and reduce hot-spot risks while preserving their appearance.

The article “Prediction Model for Power Output and Hot-spot Risk in Colored Photovoltaic Arrays with Artistic Image” has appeared in Energy. Researchers from South Korea’s Seoul National University of Science and Technology and Gachon University have participated in the study.

item.title: Australia’s battery manufacturing strength lays in component supply
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium and producing copper current collector foil, are both identified in a CSIRO report as front-runners for Australia's sovereign battery manufacturing capability.
item.content:encoded:
Prismatic battery cell cans from Australian aluminium using the impact extrusion process, and producing copper current collector foil using electrolytic deposition (ED), are both identified in a CSIRO report as front-runners for Australia’s sovereign battery manufacturing capability.

The future of Australian battery manufacturing: Cell cans and current collector foils report outlines a study focussed on the technical manufacturing processes and materials required for production of select components of lithium-ion battery cells: the battery cell cans and current collector foils used in each cell.

Comparing the requirements with known capabilities in Australia, the CSIRO researchers aimed to identify opportunities for a domestic battery supply chain

CSIRO Advanced Battery Manufacturing lead Dr Adam Best said Australia can bring more of the battery manufacturing value chain onshore.

“This would mean Australia could move beyond exporting raw and refined materials alone, towards creating higher-value products, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and strengthening supply chains for technologies that will underpin the clean energy transition,” Best said.

Battery cell cans

On battery cell cans, the report’s primary recommendation is to first consider production of prismatic format battery cells made from Australian aluminium, using the impact extrusion route.

The researchers recommend that investment be made in an aluminium slug production facility equivalent to that commissioned by Jamestrong Packaging in 2025 for $6-$8 million (USD 4-5.4 million) but tailored to the requirements of prismatic cells.

Secondly, investment should be allocated to an automated, high volume, production cell specific to impact extrusion of prismatic type battery cell cans.

Production of foils

For Australian production of foils for battery cell current collectors, a first priority would be the production of copper foil in Australia using the ED method.

The report says it is the option more likely to offer a viable commercial case compared to rolled annealed (RA) copper foil or rolled aluminium foil.

Of the six recommendations for foil production, another includes the scoping and costing of an ED copper foil facility, in line with a scalable facility to enable a smaller up-front investment to reduce the barrier to entering the market, “but also offer scope for straightforward expansion of the production capacity by adding additional parallel production cells.”

CSIRO researcher Geoff de Looze said the study focused on realistic opportunities to move from minerals and materials into higher-value components.

“Australia has many of the building blocks needed for a battery manufacturing sector,” de Looze said.

item.title: Federal government cancels panel recycling pilot, considers ‘next steps’
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The Australian government is considering 'next steps' for procuring a National Solar Panel Recycling Pilot administrator after cancelling the search on the same day an ongoing six month suspension of the procurement was also lifted.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian government is considering ‘next steps’ for procuring a National Solar Panel Recycling Pilot’ administrator, after cancelling its search the day an ongoing six month suspension was also lifted.

Undisclosed “changes to the industry” since the release of the government’s tender in April 2026, are cited as the catalyst for the decision on 10 November to cancel the procurement without the award of a contract.

Initially suspended in May 2026 due to a procurement complaint and consequent investigation, the original tender proposed that a contract for an NSPRP administrator would have begun by May 2026 and run until June 2027, with the possibility of extension.

The complaint centred on the settings and rules of the procurement process for the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW), but details are not public.

The $24.7 million (USD 16.9 million) pilot procurement sought to engage a supplier to arrange, manage, deliver and report to the government on an NSPRP.

It would be tasked with arranging the collection of up to 250,000 decommissioned panels from around 100 sites across Australia and ensure panels are safely aggregated, transported and recycled.

The government estimates 3 million panels reached end-of-life in 2025, and could grow to 50 million panels by 2035.

item.title: Ammonia corrosion resistance testing preps panels for 4.7 MW agrivoltaic project
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: TCL Solar has conducted ammonia corrosion resistance testing on TOPCon modules it supplied for an agrivoltaic dairy project in New Zealand where approximatley 700 cattle graze under the 8-hectare installation.
item.content:encoded:
China-headquartered renewable energy technology manufacturer TCL Solar has conducted ammonia corrosion resistance testing on 625W TOPCon modules it supplied for an agrivoltaic dairy project in New Zealand (NZ).

The Gordon Cattle and Solar Farm in Galatea, on the North Island, 300 kilometres southeast of Auckland, runs approximately 700 cattle, which will graze under the 2.2 metre Clenergy tracking systems.

Exposure to ammonia in an agricultural setting is a technical challenge for agrivoltaics deployed in proximity to livestock, where waste, manure and farm processes can affect susceptible materials and components within solar modules.

Potentially contributing to corrosion and reduced long-term performance, the ammonia corrosion resistance testing was done in accordance with the international standard known as IEC 62716.

Additional benefits sought by the dairy owners, beyond electricity generation, include free roaming for the cattle, shade for grazing areas, lowering of soil temperatures which helps to retain in-ground moisture, and stress relief for cattle during hot weather.

Vegetation and moisture beneath the panels may also help moderate module temperature and support energy generation.

item.title: Ausgrid energy mapping tool backs C&I community power network trial
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Ausgrid has released a digital energy mapping tool to complement its Community Power Network trial and shows where new solar, battery and energy projects would work best, based on detailed connection and curtailment data.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered electricity distributor Ausgrid has released a digital energy mapping tool to complement its Community Power Network (CPN) trial and shows where new solar, battery and energy projects would work best, based on detailed connection and curtailment data.

The data includes information on where there is capacity in the electricity network to connect more solar and batteries, areas where network limitations may exist, and locations where future energy projects may be suitable, Ausgrid said.

The CPN aims to turn commercial and industrial (C&I) rooftop solar surplus into an opportunity to share energy with consumers who don’t have solar access, such as neighbourhood renters and apartment dwellers, with the new tool pinpointing optimum opportunities for businesses deploying rooftop solar or batteries.

The spatial energy planning data tool covers three locations associated with the CPN and includes the Mascot-Botany and Northern Central Coast regions, and Caringbah in south Sydney.

Ausgrid Group External Affairs and Strategy Executive Tim Jarratt said the CPN trial explores how large C&I rooftops can be used to generate more solar energy, supported by community batteries, while sharing the financial benefits with households and businesses across local communities.

“As part of the trial, we’re making detailed information about the local electricity network publicly available to give businesses and energy providers a clearer picture of where new solar, battery and energy projects could work best,” Jarratt said.

“In Caringbah, the data will help the market to explore and test its own ideas. It’s a great opportunity to see what different approaches emerge and what we can learn from them.”

item.title: 200 MWh BESS begins commercial operation in Western Australia
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Alinta Enery has begun commercial operation of its 100 MW / 200 MWh Wagerup battery energy storage system in Western Australia, supporting the integration of renewable energy into the SWIS.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore-headquartered gentailer Alinta Enery, a 100% owned subsidiary of Sembcorp Industries, has begun commercial operation of its 100 MW / 200 MWh Wagerup battery energy storage system (BESS) in Western Australia (WA).

Supporting the integration of renewable energy into the South West Interconnected System (SWIS), the project is located approximately 120 kilometres south of Perth, adjacent to Alinta’s 392 MW gas-fired Wagerup Power Station.

Alinta Energy Merchant Energy Executive Director Ken Woolley said challenging site conditions required significant redesign and remediation, including raising the battery platform and constructing substantial retaining infrastructure.

“Despite the complexity, the team delivered an immaculate site and a critical piece of infrastructure for Western Australia,” Woolley said.

item.title: Cbus completes ‘solar skin’ to help power new 48-storey office tower
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: One of Australia’s first large-scale building-integrated solar façades is now complete with the last of almost 1,400 PV panels installed across a new $1.1 billion commercial office tower in Melbourne’s CBD.
item.content:encoded:
Australian property investor and developer Cbus Property and construction partner Multiplex have completed the installation of a 2,679 square metre building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) system that will help power the new 435 Bourke Street building in central Melbourne.

The BIPV system comprises 1,391 integrated solar panels with an installed peak capacity of 375 kW installed across the 48-storey tower’s façade, crown and rooftop. Once commissioned, design modelling estimates the system will generate up to 20% of the complex’s forecast base-building electricity requirements on site, with the balance supplied through an off-site renewable energy arrangement.

Cbus Chief Executive Officer Chris Kakoufas said the completion of the BIPV system represents “a defining moment for sustainable commercial development in Australia.”

“Successfully installing 435 Bourke Street’s solar skin is a significant achievement for our project team and partners, not to mention a tangible demonstration of how innovation and sustainability can be embraced to enhance a building’s performance while contributing to its architectural identity,” he said.

Kakoufas said the solar skin reflects an emerging approach to the use of PV technology in commercial buildings, combining on-site renewable energy generation with elements of the building’s architectural design.

“The solar facade creates electricity but also is acting as a sunshade that stops heat coming into the building and so that also reduces the electrical demand to run cooling,” he said. “This reduces operational costs for our tenant partners and emissions from grid electricity consumption, while creating a distinctive visual identity for the tower.”

Multiplex Victoria Manager Ross Snowball said installing the solar skin had been “one of the most challenging aspects of delivering the project.”

“Integrating nearly 1,400 PV panels into the building envelope required not just technical smarts but also extensive coordination between the façade, structural and services teams to ensure no impact to quality or program,” he said, adding that the project is “a great example of how early collaboration between project partners enables innovation to be embedded into the delivery of a project rather than bolted on at the end.”

Cian Davis, from architectural firm Bates Smart, acknowledged that the installation of the BIPV system required a highly complex construction process but said with the building having proven the concept, “I think you will see more like it.”

“The role of a tower façade has always been to protect the interior from the sun,” he said. “At 435 Bourke Street, it does that while also generating the building’s power …  with solar ‘leaves’ that shade the workplace as they produce energy.”

“Beyond the technology itself, the building demonstrates that energy generation can be part of a tower’s architectural expression, giving form, texture and identity to the façade, rather than sitting invisibly within it.”

Cbus said construction on 435 Bourke Street is progressing toward practical completion in late 2026. Once complete, the development will provide approximately 62,000 square metres of office accommodation.

item.title: Risen rolls out new HJT module for Australian rooftop market
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Risen Energy has unveiled a new series of dual-glass heterojunction solar panels power outputs up to 500 W and a conversion efficiency of up to 23.5% in an all-black frame.
item.content:encoded:
China-based PV module manufacturer Risen Energy has unveiled a new dual-glass bifacial heterojunction (HJT) solar module series for Australia’s residential and commercial rooftops. 

Risen said the RisenSpace module series features the company’s heterojunction (HJT) technology and zero-busbar, stress-free interconnection technology and has been “designed for Australia’s demanding climate.”

“Its introduction expands the options available to Australian households and businesses seeking long-term solar generation,” the company said.

The RisenSpace series is available in nine variants, with power outputs ranging from 460 W to 500 W, a bifacial factor of 90 ± 5%, and efficiencies from 21.6% through to 23.5%. They are made with 90 n-type HJT half-cut cells and have a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V.

The solar modules have open-circuit voltages ranging between 68.28 V and 69.56 V, along with short-circuit currents ranging from 8.56 A to 9.07 A. All versions of the bifacial module series share dimensions of 1,952 mm × 1,090 mm × 30 mm and a weight of 24 kg. They features 2 mm anti-glare heat-strengthened glass on the front and 1.6 mm heat-strengthened glass on the rear, along with a black anodised aluminum alloy frame, and an IP68-rated junction box.

Risen said the panels can operate within a temperature range of -40 C to 75 C and exhibit an operating temperature coefficient of -0.24% per degree Celsius,

“This means it loses less output as panels heat up on a summer roof — a useful trait in Australian conditions,” the manufacturer said.

Risen provides a 40-year product guarantee and a 40-year linear power output guarantee, adding the modules have a first-year degradation rate of 1%, followed by an annual degradation cap of 0.3%. After 40 years, the module is guaranteed to retain at least 87.3% of its rated output.

The new RisenSpace was launched as part of celebrations marking Risen’s 18th year in the Australian market.

The company also showcased the 760 Wp Hyper-ion Ultra module for utility-scale solar projects, saying the two modules address distinct project needs, extending the company’s HJT portfolio from rooftop installations to large-scale solar farms.

Beyond solar modules, Risen’s Australian portfolio spans utility-scale projects, residential and commercial applications, and integrated energy storage solutions.

item.title: Regulator suspends major solar and battery installer from SRES
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Prominent solar and battery installer and retailer Solar Power Nation has been banned by the Clean Energy Regulator from participating in Australia’s small scale renewable energy rebate scheme.
item.content:encoded:
The Clean Energy Regulator (CER) announced it has permanently suspended solar retailer 1 Solar Australia Pty Ltd, trading as Solar Power Nation, as a registered person under the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES).

The CER said it is no longer satisfied that the Sydney-based company meets the “fit and proper” person requirements, meaning the company can no longer operate as a registered agent under the SRES or create the small-scale technology certificates (STCs) needed to access federal government rebates.

“If we see companies that are not operating professionally, we will not hesitate to take action to protect the integrity of the SRES,” CER Chair Tony Chappel said. “We have a zero-tolerance approach for any poor business practice that can create an adverse outcome for the customer.”

The CER’s move comes after Solar Power Nation, which sells rooftop solar and battery systems in five states and is endorsed by sporting celebrities including former Australian cricket captain Michael Clarke, was subject to multiple investigations.

The ABC earlier this year reported the installer and retailer was under investigation in Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and South Australia after authorities received hundreds of complaints dating back to 2024. The complaints ranged from allegations of unfinished or defective work to unrefunded deposit payments for installs that never happened.

NSW’s Building Commission, which regulates the building and electrical work for solar and battery installations in that state, said it had received more than 240 complaints about the company.

The Commissioner for Consumer Affairs in South Australia has issued a Public Warning Notice about Solar Power Nation and late last year it was expelled as an approved seller under from the industry-run New Energy Tech Consumer Code (NETCC) for breaches relating to contract issues and safety and installation standards. The NETCC, administered by the Clean Energy Council (CEC), oversees approved sellers with standards for advertising, sales practices, installations and complaint handling.

Chappel said the work of other industry bodies and the outcomes of their investigations had helped inform the CER decision.

“We work closely with consumer protection agencies, industry bodies and other regulators to share intelligence and identify and address any systemic risks within the solar and battery industry,” he said.

1 Solar Australia has 60 days to request a review of the CER’s decision.

The company was contacted for comment but did not receive one prior to publication.
